word:lxx:L700163.explanation: This word means “arm,” referring to the limb extending from the shoulder and used in ordinary bodily description. word:lxx:L700264.explanation: This adjective describes someone who is headstrong—firmly determined to follow their own will rather than readily accept guidance or correction. It presents a person as difficult to turn or persuade, emphasizing stubborn self-direction. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in Sirach. Its basic sense is therefore a characterization of a person’s resistant, self-willed disposition, while the surrounding verse determines the specific situation in which that quality is being described.

word:lxx:L700497.explanation: This Greek LXX adverb means “suddenly,” describing something that happens unexpectedly or without warning. word:lxx:L700570.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to “sharpen” or “whet”—to make something sharp. It describes an action rather than an object, person, or quality. This word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX data, appearing in Psalms and Proverbs. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the action of sharpening.

word:lxx:L700633.explanation: This adjective describes someone who is “speechless; dumb”—unable to express words aloud. It refers to a lack of speech rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice, both times in Psalms, so its basic meaning is clear but its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. It is used in Psalms 30:19 and 37:14.

word:lxx:L700668.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to a person called Aliel or Alil. word:lxx:L700893.explanation: Amoth is a proper name, referring to a specific person or place rather than expressing a general idea or action. word:lxx:L701177.explanation: Annan is a personal name used to identify an individual in the Greek Old Testament text. word:lxx:L701199.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as “irresponsible.” It presents conduct or character negatively, identifying a lack of responsibility rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. word:lxx:L701209.explanation: This noun means “in exchange”: something offered or received in place of something else. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being exchanged and the surrounding words.

word:lxx:L701245.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to denounce or contradict. It describes speaking against someone, rejecting what has been said, or openly opposing a claim. word:lxx:L701292.explanation: This adjective describes something that cannot be successfully resisted: it is “not to be withstood” or “irresistible.” It can characterize a force, action, or power that opposition cannot overcome. word:lxx:L701344.explanation: This verb means to make someone rise up and depart, or to send someone away. It describes movement away from a place or the act of causing another person to leave. word:lxx:L701418.explanation: This adjective describes something “not to be filled” or “insatiate”—a condition that remains unsatisfied rather than becoming full. word:lxx:L701443.explanation: This verb means “bind”: to fasten, tie, or hold something so it is not free to move. It describes an action rather than a person or object. word:lxx:L701627.explanation: This verb means “fail in hitting”—to miss the intended target rather than strike it. word:lxx:L704026.explanation: Edeia is a proper name, also represented as Ethia. It functions as a personal designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L704080.explanation: This interjection expresses a strong wish or longing, meaning “would that!” It introduces something the speaker desires to happen or be true. word:lxx:L713376.explanation: Pharphar, also rendered Farfar, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or abstract idea. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament translation. This name occurs once in the LXX, at 2 Kings 5:12. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise role in that passage cannot be described further; the supported lexical meaning is simply the name Pharphar or Farfar.

word:lxx:L713505.explanation: φιλοφρόνως means “amicably”: it describes speaking or acting in a friendly, peaceable way toward someone. As an adverb, it tells how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense describes conduct marked by goodwill and courteous friendliness, while the surrounding verse determines the precise action it describes.

word:lxx:L713642.explanation: Phōs means light. In the creation account, light appears when God commands it to exist.

word:lxx:L713710.explanation: Chanana, also rendered Khanana, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named Chanana. This name occurs five times, in five verses, across 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, and 2 Chronicles. Its precise significance as a personal name is not defined by the available passages, so it is best understood simply as the name Chanana or Khanana.

word:lxx:L714135.explanation: This noun means “elegance” or “adornment”—something that gives beauty, attractiveness, or a pleasing appearance. It can describe outward beauty or the way something is made appealing. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Jeremiah 4:30, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains the quality or decoration that makes someone or something appear beautiful or attractive.
